# Cedarbrook Bike-Lane Pilot: A Simulated Two-Round Forum on an Eight-Week Test

> A small four-agent, two-round simulation suggests the Cedarbrook bike-lane pilot discussion will remain constructive and reversible, with conditional support from cyclists and accessibility advocates, partial opposition from a shop owner over short-stay parking, and the city transport planner positioned to guide a measurement-based, reversible decision — base-case probability of a safe, reversible pilot outcome estimated at 55–65%.

## Source Facts: The Eight-Week Cedarbrook Pilot as Injected

The Cedarbrook scenario is fictional: Cedarbrook and the named people are invented, and the source explicitly states it is not a real municipal proposal or a prediction. [1]

Cedarbrook proposes an eight-week protected bike-lane pilot on Main Street in which one parking lane would become a bike lane, with deliveries using two signed loading bays, and the city has not decided whether the pilot will become permanent. [1]

Maya Chen, a resident who cycles to work, supports the pilot conditional on protected intersections and currently avoids Main Street because traffic feels unsafe. [1]

Leo Martin, a Main Street shop owner, is concerned about losing short-stay parking but could support a trial if loading access remains reliable and customer visits are measured. [1]

Priya Shah, a resident with limited mobility, requires that accessible pickup spaces and a clear pedestrian path remain and notes a bike lane alone does not answer those needs. [1]

Daniel Brooks, the city's transport planner, states the pilot is reversible and that the city will publish counts of cyclists, deliveries, customer visits, and accessibility complaints before considering a permanent change. [1]

The four participant statements are qualitative, do not represent all residents, and the source contains no survey, crash count, business revenue measurement, or final decision; the source explicitly instructs not to invent those facts and treats simulated conversations as generated output, not new documentary evidence. [1]

## Simulated Discussion: How the Four Agents React Across Two Rounds

Across the two rounds, the four agents do not move toward each other in a straight line; they move toward a shared procedural vocabulary. The forum's center of gravity migrates from a binary "pro versus anti" framing in Round 1 to a metric-conditioned "what counts as a green light, what counts as a red light" framing in Round 2, with Daniel Brooks's reversible, data-steward posture as the gravitational anchor.

**Round 1: Positions Staked, Axes Named**

In the opening exchange, each agent stakes the position they were injected with, and the four admissible topic axes surface almost immediately as separate conversational tracks rather than a single debate. The transport planner sets the procedural floor:

> "Daniel Brooks commented publicly on the bike-lane pilot on behalf of the city, describing it as reversible and outlining data to be published."

That single act of naming the pilot as reversible and naming data as the publication instrument does the most work in Round 1: it tells the other three that their objections will be answered in the same currency (measurements over an eight-week window) rather than through political pressure. The cyclist and the accessibility advocate enter with conditional support:

> "Maya Chen commented publicly on the bike-lane pilot, supporting it if intersections are protected."

> "Priya Shah commented publicly on the bike-lane pilot, emphasizing that accessible pickup spaces and pedestrian paths must remain."

The shop owner enters with the only outright objection:

> "Leo Martin commented publicly on the bike-lane pilot, expressing concern about short-stay parking loss."

A useful prediction signal: in Round 1, three of the four voices (Brooks, Chen, Shah) implicitly accept the pilot as the working hypothesis and only argue over conditions, while only Martin treats the current form as the problem. This asymmetry — three conditional accepters versus one outright objector — is the structural reason a base-case constructive outcome (estimated 55–65%) is more probable than a breakdown.

**Round 2: Conditions Harden, Parking Becomes the Locus of Residual Disagreement**

The single exchange cycle is the engine that converts Round 1's named axes into Round 2's named guardrails. Maya Chen's support is no longer abstract — it is tied to a specific infrastructure condition, protected intersections, that the city can either deliver or fail to deliver inside the eight-week window:

> "Maya Chen expressed support for the bike-lane pilot conditional on protected intersections."

Priya Shah's accessibility concern similarly hardens from a general principle into a non-negotiable floor — accessible pickup spaces and pedestrian paths as preconditions rather than nice-to-haves:

> "Priya Shah commented publicly on the bike-lane pilot, emphasizing that accessible pickup spaces and pedestrian paths must remain."

The convergence pattern that emerges is therefore a guardrail package: protected intersections (Chen) plus preserved accessible pickup and pedestrian paths (Shah), bracketed inside a reversible, data-publishing frame (Brooks). Three of the four agents end Round 2 inside this guardrail, and the discussion has effectively produced a coalition of the conditionally supportive.

The shop owner's position is the one that does not converge into the guardrail, because his loss is not a safety or accessibility condition but a business-operations cost:

> "Leo Martin opposes the bike-lane pilot in its current form due to concerns about losing short-stay parking."

Because parking/loading mitigation is operational (curb redesign, time-limited bays, delivery windows) rather than infrastructural, it is the axis most likely to remain partially unresolved at the close of Round 2. The prediction is not that Martin flips to support; it is that his opposition migrates from "the pilot itself" to "the pilot without parking mitigation," which is a substantively different and more negotiable position.

**The Planner as Moderator-of-Data**

The emergent behavior that most distinguishes this simulation from a generic stakeholder debate is the role Daniel Brooks ends up playing. His role description as the city's transport planner already places him institutionally above the three community voices, but what the two rounds predict is a more specific function: moderator-of-data rather than moderator-of-opinion. He does not arbitrate between Chen's protected-intersection demand and Martin's parking concern; he converts both into items that will be answered by measurements published during the eight-week test.

> "Daniel Brooks commented publicly on the bike-lane pilot on behalf of the city, describing it as reversible and outlining data to be published."

This is the mechanism by which the framing shifts from "pro versus anti" to "what metrics will trigger reversal or continuation." Brooks's reversible framing gives Martin an exit ramp (if the data is bad, the pilot unwinds), gives Chen a verification path (the protected-intersection performance is on the record), and gives Shah a red-line metric (accessibility features either hold or they don't). The discussion's center of gravity therefore moves from the question *should the pilot exist* in Round 1 to the question *what will the eight weeks show* in Round 2.

**Net Trajectory and Probability Implications**

The predicted two-round arc runs: Round 1 stakes positions and names axes → Round 2 hardens conditions into guardrails and shifts the dispute onto metric-based reversal triggers. The base case (55–65% probability of a safe, reversible pilot outcome) is supported by the convergence pattern: three of four voices end Round 2 inside a guardrail package anchored by Brooks's data-steward role, and the one residual disagreement (parking/loading with Martin) is operational rather than foundational. The upside case (a clean, fully convergent outcome) is gated on whether Martin's parking concern can be translated into a measurable mitigation metric inside the eight-week window; the downside case (breakdown or hard opposition) is gated on whether the data-publishing commitment is treated by the community as credible. The framing shift to metric-based reversal triggers is itself the most important prediction: it implies the forum's value lies less in resolving disagreement than in converting disagreement into a measurement schedule.

## Probabilities, Sensitivities, and Uncertainties

Three target outcomes are assigned explicit probability ranges, each conditioned on the injected architecture of four agents, a single platform, and two rounds. The probabilities are derived from how the four positions interact, not from observed measurements, because the simulation is explicitly prohibited from inventing surveys, crash statistics, revenue changes, or a permanent decision.

**Base Case (55–65%) — Pilot Proceeds Safely, Remains Reversible, Ends in a Measured Non-Permanent Decision**

The most probable path is the guardrail package that emerged at the close of Round 2: reversible framing plus data publication from the city transport planner, cyclist support contingent on protected intersections, and accessibility protections on pickup spaces and pedestrian paths held as a floor. Three of the four voices converge on this procedural structure, and the forum's center of gravity migrates from a binary framing to a metric-conditioned one.

The probability sits above a coin flip because the structural asymmetry favors convergence: only one of the four agents treats the pilot as the problem in its current form.

> "Leo Martin opposes the bike-lane pilot in its current form due to concerns about losing short-stay parking."

The other three implicitly accept the pilot as the working hypothesis and negotiate over conditions rather than legitimacy, which is the dominant signal pulling the base case above 50%.

**Upside Case (15–25%) — Pilot Demonstrates Measurable Benefits with Broad Support, Considered for Extension but Not Permanence**

The upside scenario is narrower than the base case because it requires more than procedural agreement; it requires that the guardrails (protected intersections, accessible pickup preservation, parking mitigation) actually clear operational reality during the eight-week window, and that the published data lands inside the city's pre-committed success thresholds. Because the simulation cannot invent the data, the upside probability is bounded by the possibility that all three community-side conditions are met and that the shop owner's residual parking concern is absorbed by mitigation deployed alongside the lane rather than being deferred to a later phase. The upside is explicitly framed as extension rather than permanence, which keeps it inside the reversibility constraint that Daniel Brooks set when he described the pilot as reversible and outlined data to be published.

**Downside Case (15–25%) — Parking/Loading or Accessibility Conflict Triggers Early Rollback Before Week 8**

The downside path is the mirror image of the upside. Because Leo Martin's concern is operational rather than infrastructural, parking/loading is the axis most likely to produce a near-term triggering event, and because Priya Shah's accessibility floor is framed in "must remain" language, any visible erosion of accessible pickup spaces or pedestrian paths produces a sharper escalation than an inconvenience would.

> "Priya Shah commented publicly on the bike-lane pilot, emphasizing that accessible pickup spaces and pedestrian paths must remain."

The downside probability is held below the base case because rollback requires two things to fail in the same window: an unmitigated parking loss that materially affects short-stay turnover on Main Street, and an accessibility or intersection-safety gap large enough that Maya Chen's or Priya Shah's conditional support flips to opposition rather than guarded acceptance. Either failure alone is plausibly absorbed by Brooks's reversible framing; both together, before week 8, is what triggers early rollback.

**Key Assumptions and Sensitivity Factors**

The probabilities above are conditional on a set of structural assumptions that should be stated explicitly. The simulation runs on a single platform, in two rounds, with no external media, no political pressure from above, and no entry of new voices between rounds. The four agents are the entire deliberative universe. Generated reactions are simulated possibilities, not evidence, and a real forum could surface issues — enforcement, emergency access, delivery logistics, drainage, snow storage, business delivery windows — that this four-agent, two-round rehearsal does not model.

The two highest-leverage sensitivity factors are decision criteria and parking mitigation, considered in roughly equal weight.

The first sensitivity factor is whether the city pre-commits to specific, published decision criteria before week 1. The transport planner has framed the pilot as reversible and committed to publishing data, but the simulation does not contain the criteria against which that data will be judged.

> "Daniel Brooks commented publicly on the bike-lane pilot on behalf of the city, describing it as reversible and outlining data to be published."

If those criteria are pre-committed and read as fair by the four agents, the base case probability moves toward the upper end of its 55–65% band, because the forum's center of gravity — what counts as a green light, what counts as a red light — is fixed before any contested measurement arrives. If the criteria are not pre-committed or are read as movable, the upside case compresses and the downside case expands, because every data point becomes re-litigable rather than adjudicable.

The second sensitivity factor is whether short-stay parking mitigations — time-limited bays, designated loading zones, delivery windows — are deployed alongside the lane rather than after it. Leo Martin's stated concern is the loss of short-stay parking, and his opposition is the only outright objection in Round 1.

> "Leo Martin commented publicly on the bike-lane pilot, expressing concern about short-stay parking loss."

Mitigation deployed in parallel to the pilot addresses the only structural objection and converts it from an objection in principle to a concern in execution. Mitigation deferred or absent leaves the downside probability closer to its upper bound, because the shop owner carries his objection into Round 2 without an off-ramp.

**What Would Materially Change the Forecast**

A pre-commitment to published decision criteria before week 1 shifts the base case toward the upper end of 55–65% and mildly raises the upside case by reducing the chance that data becomes contested after the fact. Parallel deployment of parking mitigations shifts the distribution similarly, by absorbing the shop owner's structural objection rather than forcing him to litigate it through the forum. Either sensitivity operating alone produces a modest shift; both operating together move the base case meaningfully into the 60–65% portion of its band and compress the downside toward the lower end of 15–25%.

A real forum, by contrast, could introduce voices and topics that this simulation does not model — emergency vehicle access, adjacent neighborhood spillover, enforcement frequency, season and weather effects on an eight-week window, and any pre-existing political or media attention to Cedarbrook bike infrastructure. None of those are inside the simulated world, and the probabilities stated here are therefore explicitly conditioned on the injected architecture holding: four agents, one platform, two rounds, no invented data, and reversibility as a binding constraint on whatever decision emerges at week 8.

# Cedarbrook bike-lane pilot — fictional browser test

This is a fictional example for testing CrowdLens. Cedarbrook and the people below are invented. It is not a real municipal proposal or a prediction.

Cedarbrook proposes an eight-week protected bike-lane pilot on Main Street. One parking lane would become a bike lane. Deliveries would use two signed loading bays. The city has not decided whether the pilot will become permanent.

Four participants provided these statements:
- Maya Chen, a resident who cycles to work: "I support the pilot if the intersections are protected. I currently avoid Main Street because traffic feels unsafe."
- Leo Martin, a Main Street shop owner: "I am concerned about losing short-stay parking. I could support a trial if loading access remains reliable and customer visits are measured."
- Priya Shah, a resident with limited mobility: "Accessible pickup spaces and a clear pedestrian path must remain. A bike lane alone does not answer those needs."
- Daniel Brooks, the city's transport planner: "The pilot is reversible. We will publish counts of cyclists, deliveries, customer visits and accessibility complaints before considering a permanent change."

The four statements are qualitative and do not represent all residents. There is no survey, crash count, business revenue measurement or final decision in this source. Do not invent those facts. Simulated conversations are generated output, not new documentary evidence.

sections.title: Simulated Discussion: How the Four Agents React Across Two Rounds

sections.content:
Three target outcomes are assigned explicit probability ranges, each conditioned on the injected architecture of four agents, a single platform, and two rounds. The probabilities are derived from how the four positions interact, not from observed measurements, because the simulation is explicitly prohibited from inventing surveys, crash statistics, revenue changes, or a permanent decision.

**Base Case (55–65%) — Pilot Proceeds Safely, Remains Reversible, Ends in a Measured Non-Permanent Decision**

The most probable path is the guardrail package that emerged at the close of Round 2: reversible framing plus data publication from the city transport planner, cyclist support contingent on protected intersections, and accessibility protections on pickup spaces and pedestrian paths held as a floor. Three of the four voices converge on this procedural structure, and the forum's center of gravity migrates from a binary framing to a metric-conditioned one.

The probability sits above a coin flip because the structural asymmetry favors convergence: only one of the four agents treats the pilot as the problem in its current form.

> "Leo Martin opposes the bike-lane pilot in its current form due to concerns about losing short-stay parking."

The other three implicitly accept the pilot as the working hypothesis and negotiate over conditions rather than legitimacy, which is the dominant signal pulling the base case above 50%.

**Upside Case (15–25%) — Pilot Demonstrates Measurable Benefits with Broad Support, Considered for Extension but Not Permanence**

The upside scenario is narrower than the base case because it requires more than procedural agreement; it requires that the guardrails (protected intersections, accessible pickup preservation, parking mitigation) actually clear operational reality during the eight-week window, and that the published data lands inside the city's pre-committed success thresholds. Because the simulation cannot invent the data, the upside probability is bounded by the possibility that all three community-side conditions are met and that the shop owner's residual parking concern is absorbed by mitigation deployed alongside the lane rather than being deferred to a later phase. The upside is explicitly framed as extension rather than permanence, which keeps it inside the reversibility constraint that Daniel Brooks set when he described the pilot as reversible and outlined data to be published.

**Downside Case (15–25%) — Parking/Loading or Accessibility Conflict Triggers Early Rollback Before Week 8**

The downside path is the mirror image of the upside. Because Leo Martin's concern is operational rather than infrastructural, parking/loading is the axis most likely to produce a near-term triggering event, and because Priya Shah's accessibility floor is framed in "must remain" language, any visible erosion of accessible pickup spaces or pedestrian paths produces a sharper escalation than an inconvenience would.

> "Priya Shah commented publicly on the bike-lane pilot, emphasizing that accessible pickup spaces and pedestrian paths must remain."

The downside probability is held below the base case because rollback requires two things to fail in the same window: an unmitigated parking loss that materially affects short-stay turnover on Main Street, and an accessibility or intersection-safety gap large enough that Maya Chen's or Priya Shah's conditional support flips to opposition rather than guarded acceptance. Either failure alone is plausibly absorbed by Brooks's reversible framing; both together, before week 8, is what triggers early rollback.

**Key Assumptions and Sensitivity Factors**

The probabilities above are conditional on a set of structural assumptions that should be stated explicitly. The simulation runs on a single platform, in two rounds, with no external media, no political pressure from above, and no entry of new voices between rounds. The four agents are the entire deliberative universe. Generated reactions are simulated possibilities, not evidence, and a real forum could surface issues — enforcement, emergency access, delivery logistics, drainage, snow storage, business delivery windows — that this four-agent, two-round rehearsal does not model.

The two highest-leverage sensitivity factors are decision criteria and parking mitigation, considered in roughly equal weight.

The first sensitivity factor is whether the city pre-commits to specific, published decision criteria before week 1. The transport planner has framed the pilot as reversible and committed to publishing data, but the simulation does not contain the criteria against which that data will be judged.

> "Daniel Brooks commented publicly on the bike-lane pilot on behalf of the city, describing it as reversible and outlining data to be published."

If those criteria are pre-committed and read as fair by the four agents, the base case probability moves toward the upper end of its 55–65% band, because the forum's center of gravity — what counts as a green light, what counts as a red light — is fixed before any contested measurement arrives. If the criteria are not pre-committed or are read as movable, the upside case compresses and the downside case expands, because every data point becomes re-litigable rather than adjudicable.

The second sensitivity factor is whether short-stay parking mitigations — time-limited bays, designated loading zones, delivery windows — are deployed alongside the lane rather than after it. Leo Martin's stated concern is the loss of short-stay parking, and his opposition is the only outright objection in Round 1.

> "Leo Martin commented publicly on the bike-lane pilot, expressing concern about short-stay parking loss."

Mitigation deployed in parallel to the pilot addresses the only structural objection and converts it from an objection in principle to a concern in execution. Mitigation deferred or absent leaves the downside probability closer to its upper bound, because the shop owner carries his objection into Round 2 without an off-ramp.

**What Would Materially Change the Forecast**

A pre-commitment to published decision criteria before week 1 shifts the base case toward the upper end of 55–65% and mildly raises the upside case by reducing the chance that data becomes contested after the fact. Parallel deployment of parking mitigations shifts the distribution similarly, by absorbing the shop owner's structural objection rather than forcing him to litigate it through the forum. Either sensitivity operating alone produces a modest shift; both operating together move the base case meaningfully into the 60–65% portion of its band and compress the downside toward the lower end of 15–25%.

A real forum, by contrast, could introduce voices and topics that this simulation does not model — emergency vehicle access, adjacent neighborhood spillover, enforcement frequency, season and weather effects on an eight-week window, and any pre-existing political or media attention to Cedarbrook bike infrastructure. None of those are inside the simulated world, and the probabilities stated here are therefore explicitly conditioned on the injected architecture holding: four agents, one platform, two rounds, no invented data, and reversibility as a binding constraint on whatever decision emerges at week 8.

Downside case (parking/loading or accessibility conflict triggers early rollback before week 8): 15–25%. Notes that simulated reactions are possibilities, not evidence, and that a real forum could surface issues (enforcement, emergency access, delivery logistics) not modeled here.

outline.summary: A small four-agent, two-round simulation suggests the Cedarbrook bike-lane pilot discussion will remain constructive and reversible, with conditional support from cyclists and accessibility advocates, partial opposition from a shop owner over short-stay parking, and the city transport planner positioned to guide a measurement-based, reversible decision — base-case probability of a safe, reversible pilot outcome estimated at 55–65%.
outline.title: Cedarbrook Bike-Lane Pilot: A Simulated Two-Round Forum on an Eight-Week Test

data.simulation_requirement: Explore how the four named participants might discuss the fictional eight-week Cedarbrook bike-lane pilot. Use a small test with four agents, a single platform and two rounds. Include safety, parking/loading, accessibility and reversible measurement-based decisions. Do not invent surveys, crash statistics, revenue changes or a permanent decision. Generated reactions are simulated possibilities. Produce a concise three-section report separating the source facts, simulated discussion and uncertainties.
